title: Greece Beyond Santorini: The Islands Worth Your Ferry Ticket
metaDescription: A guide to Greece’s less-crowded islands — Milos, Naxos, Folegandros, Sifnos, Karpathos and more — with ferry logistics and how to combine them.
excerpt: Santorini and Mykonos absorb most of Greece’s visitors. There are roughly 200 inhabited islands, and some of the best are almost empty.
author: Travel Editors
content:
Greece has around 200 inhabited islands. A very large share of visitors go to two of them.

Santorini's caldera is genuinely unique and Mykonos does what it does extremely well, but both are operating at capacity, with cruise arrivals managed by quota and sunset viewing that involves a crowd. Meanwhile, islands a ferry hop away have the same water, better beaches, better food and a fraction of the people.

Here is where to go instead, organised by what you actually want.

## If You Want Dramatic Landscapes: Milos

The strongest single recommendation in the Cyclades.

Milos is volcanic, like Santorini, but the geology expressed itself differently — instead of a caldera, you get an extraordinary variety of coastline. **Sarakiniko** is a moonscape of white volcanic rock sculpted by wind into something that looks synthetic. **Kleftiko** is a set of sea caves reachable only by boat. **Firiplaka** and **Tsigrado** are dramatic cliff-backed beaches, and there are over seventy beaches in total, many of them different in colour and texture.

Add **Plaka** for a hilltop sunset, the fishing village of **Klima** with its coloured boathouses, and catacombs from the early Christian era.

Milos has become popular and is still nothing like Santorini.

## If You Want Beaches and Food: Naxos

The largest Cycladic island and the most self-sufficient — it has real agriculture, which means the food is genuinely local rather than shipped in.

The west coast has the best beaches in the Cyclades: **Plaka**, **Agios Prokopios** and **Agia Anna** are long sand beaches with shallow, clear water, and they are large enough to absorb visitors without feeling crowded.

Inland, the **mountain villages** — Halki, Apeiranthos, Filoti — are stone-built and largely unaffected by tourism, with Mount Zas walkable from Filoti. The **kouros** statues, abandoned unfinished in ancient quarries, are a strange and memorable sight. The Portara, a freestanding marble doorway on the harbour islet, frames the sunset.

Naxos is the best island for families and for anyone staying a week or more.

![Greece travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1575540291670-8d3b26f7d327?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## If You Want the Clifftop Village Without the Crowd: Folegandros

Small, quiet, and with a main town — **Chora** — perched on a 200-metre cliff that rivals anything in Santorini for drama.

There are few beaches, most reached by boat or on foot, and little to do beyond walking, swimming and eating. That is the appeal. The hike up to the **Panagia church** above Chora at sunset is one of the best simple pleasures in the Cyclades.

Folegandros is for people who want quiet rather than activity.

## If You Want Food Above Everything: Sifnos

Widely considered the best food island in Greece, with a serious culinary tradition, a pottery heritage and slow-cooked chickpea dishes baked in clay.

Also: a beautiful clifftop monastery at **Chrysopigi**, a network of well-maintained walking trails linking villages, and the whitewashed village of **Kastro** on a rocky outcrop.

## If You Want Somewhere Genuinely Remote: Karpathos

Between Crete and Rhodes, and far enough from everything that it never became a major destination.

**Olympos**, in the north, is a village where traditional dress is still worn by older residents and the dialect preserves archaic features. The beaches are excellent and windy — Karpathos is a serious windsurfing destination. Getting there requires a flight or a long ferry, which is precisely why it stays quiet.

## If You Want History and Scale: Crete

Large enough to be a destination in itself rather than an island stop.

- **The Samaria Gorge** — a 16km walk through a spectacular gorge to the sea
- **Knossos and the Heraklion museum** — the Minoan civilisation
- **Chania and Rethymno** — Venetian old towns
- **Balos and Elafonisi** — pink-tinged sand and lagoons, busy but genuinely beautiful
- **The south coast** — Loutro, reachable only by boat or on foot, and one of the most relaxing places in Greece
- **Food** — Cretan cuisine stands on its own

![Greece travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1628095136549-f574c711d3cd?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## Other Islands Worth Knowing

- **Amorgos** — dramatic, with a monastery built into a cliff face and excellent hiking
- **Serifos and Kythnos** — close to Athens, low-key, real
- **Ikaria** — a Blue Zone island with an unusual relationship to time and a strong local culture
- **Symi** — a neoclassical harbour of coloured houses, arguably the prettiest arrival in Greece
- **Hydra** — no cars at all, an hour and a half from Athens, elegant and walkable
- **Paros and Antiparos** — busier than the above, still considerably calmer than Mykonos
- **Lefkada and the Ionians** — reachable by road, with the extraordinary beaches of Porto Katsiki and Egremni
- **Alonnisos and the Sporades** — a marine national park, green, and very quiet

## Ferry Logistics: The Thing That Decides Your Itinerary

This is where island-hopping trips go wrong.

**Ferries run within island groups, not between them.** The Cyclades connect well to each other; getting from a Cycladic island to a Dodecanese island often means routing back through Athens. Plan within one group.

**Check the actual timetable for your dates before booking accommodation.** Schedules change seasonally and some routes run only twice a week outside July and August. A route that exists in August may not exist in May.

**Book ahead in July and August**, particularly for vehicles and for popular routes.

**Weather cancels ferries.** The **meltemi** — a strong northerly wind that blows through the Aegean in July and August — regularly cancels sailings, sometimes for a day or two. **Never plan to take a ferry on the day of an international flight.** Return to Athens a day early. This is the single most important logistical rule in Greek island travel.

**High-speed versus conventional ferries** — high-speed costs roughly double and halves the time, but is cancelled more readily in wind. Conventional ferries are slower, cheaper and more reliable.

**Three islands in ten days is the right pace.** Four is possible. Five is a ferry schedule with beaches attached.

## When to Go

- **Late May to mid-June** — warm, green, everything open, the sea just about warm enough
- **September** — the best month. The sea is at its warmest of the year, the crowds have gone, prices drop
- **Early October** — still lovely, with the smaller islands beginning to wind down
- **July and August** — hot, crowded, expensive, and the meltemi is at its strongest
- **November to April** — many small islands largely close. Crete, Rhodes and the larger islands stay open

## A Ten-Day Cycladic Route

- **Days 1–2** — Athens
- **Days 3–5** — Milos
- **Days 6–8** — Folegandros or Sifnos
- **Days 9–10** — Naxos, then back to Athens

Or, for a slower trip: Naxos for six nights and Milos for four, with nothing else.

Ferry timetables are the actual constraint on any Greek island trip, and they are the thing most people check last. Work out the sailings first, build the island order around them, and leave the buffer day before your flight home. Laying it out in a shared plan on **Trypinn** makes the connections visible — and makes it obvious when a route needs a backtrack through Athens that nobody had accounted for.
